extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers interested in moral philosophy and Montaigne's essays
extracted.subtask_description: A moral-philosophical essay (Montaigne) discussing the nature of glory, reputation, virtue, and presumption, offering behavioural maxims, examples, and literary quotations as guidance for personal conduct and self-knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue not to be grounded in glory
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue is a very vain and frivolous thing if it derive its recommendation from glory; it is wrong to seek virtue primarily for reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: "Virtue is a very vain and frivolous thing if it derive its recommendation from glory; and 'tis to no purpose that we endeavour to give it a station by itself..." Examples and explanation: reputation is accidental and ruled by fortune (quoting Sallust); glory often goes before merit and is like a shadow; many brave acts are buried and unrecorded, so virtue should not be pursued for public renown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act rightly even when unobserved
rubrics_metrics.description: One must do well regardless of public notice; conscience is the sufficient reward and 'trumpet' for one's actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carneades example: if you know of a serpent lurking and expect advantage from another's death, you do ill if you don't warn him—"so much the more because the action is to be known by none but thyself." The text repeats that 'the testimony of our conscience' is our rejoicing and that a man must be valiant for himself, not for witnesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let public opinion govern conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unreasonable to let the life of a wise man depend upon the judgment of fools; one should follow reason rather than the fluctuating approbation of the multitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotations: Cicero and others on the instability of the multitude's mind. Practical advice: do not aim at a "floating and wavering" end; let public approbation follow if it will, but base action on reason and tested utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: The reward of a well-done action is the action itself
rubrics_metrics.description: The true recompense of a virtuous act is having done it; the fruit of duty is the duty itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seneca quote: "Recte facti, fecisse merces est: officii fructus, ipsum officium est." Guidance: do not exchange the intrinsic value of duty for the extrinsic value of fame; the service itself should be the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputation and fame are accidental and fleeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Fame depends on fortune and chance; many courageous deeds never become known, and historical memory is partial and precarious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Caesar and Alexander owe renown largely to fortune; many brave men die unremembered; records and histories are incomplete — 'tis fortune that gives them a shorter or longer life. Advice: do not throw away true life for a few years of imagined celebrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek inner tranquillity; live 'in quiet' by oneself
rubrics_metrics.description: One should aim for personal tranquillity that suits oneself rather than adopt a philosophical system because it is fashionable; find quiet in particular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne: 'All the glory that I pretend to derive from my life is that I have lived it in quiet... let every one seek it in particular.' Practical orientation: prioritize inner peace over public display or doctrinal conformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not cultivate honour merely as outward show or ceremony
rubrics_metrics.description: Ceremony and outward appearances corrupt true substance; they make people abandon the substance of things for branches and externals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observations: ceremony forbids speaking plainly, creates hypocrisy (e.g., in war a man can counterfeit bravery); emperors' rigid gestures are cited as artificial deportment. Advice: beware of artificial salutations and public forms that confer undeserved credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hypocrisy and false honour
rubrics_metrics.description: False honour pleases and calumny frightens the guilty; external signs of honour may mask cowardice or vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes: Horace and others on 'false honour.' Example: soldiers who counterfeit bravery; the Platonic ring example suggesting many would hide if they could. Advice: value internal courage and honesty over external honours that may be deceptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: It is acceptable to cultivate public honours and beliefs if they keep people virtuous
rubrics_metrics.description: If public opinion, myths, or ceremonial foppery help to maintain public duty and virtue, they may be tolerated and even fostered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nuance: Montaigne acknowledges that legislators have always used fabulous origins and supernatural validation to curb behaviour and promote virtue (Numa, Zoroaster, etc.). He permits cultivating favorable public reputations when they practically encourage good conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Women: do not mistake duty for 'honour'
rubrics_metrics.description: Ladies should not call that 'honour' which is merely their duty; duty is the mark, honour the outward rind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice to women: intentions and will (private) matter more than outward effects; the offence in conscience would be as great to desire as to do the forbidden act. Montaigne urges women to prefer conscience over reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid presumption — beware of an overly good opinion of oneself
rubrics_metrics.description: Having too high an opinion of our own worth is an inconsiderate affection that misrepresents us to ourselves and breeds false opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opening of Chapter XVII: presumption is likened to passion of love that lends graces to the object. Montaigne nonetheless warns against the opposite error: one should not think oneself less than one is; the judgement ought to maintain its rights. Guidance: strive for accurate self-knowledge rather than inflated self-regard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain balanced self-knowledge (avoid both over- and under-estimation)
rubrics_metrics.description: One should discern oneself aright — neither arrogate too much nor deny one's true merits; judgment must maintain its rights and see truth in oneself as in others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne: 'I would not... that a man should not know himself aright, or think himself less than he is.' Examples: public figures can manifest worth by public actions; ordinary people may reasonably speak for themselves to those interested. Practical guidance: cultivate honest self-portraiture (Lucilius committed actions/thoughts to paper).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combat possessive contempt — do not undervalue your own possessions or merits
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession breeds contempt: we often value foreign, absent, or non-owned things more highly than our own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne confesses a tendency to prize his neighbour's possessions above his own and to be swayed by Latin's dignity; practical advice: be aware of bias that makes us devalue what is ours merely because it is ours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poets must not be mediocre — mediocrity in poets is intolerable
rubrics_metrics.description: Mediocrity is not permitted in poets; bad poets are excessively confident and should be barred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotations: Horace 'Neither men, nor gods... permit mediocrity in poets.' Martial: 'nothing is more confident than a bad poet.' Montaigne's humorous injunction that this motto be written over printers' doors to 'forbid the entrance of so many rhymesters.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Civic examples and records matter to posterity, but are rare
rubrics_metrics.description: Only very eminent actions or the favour of fortune secure a place in public records; ordinary brave deeds are unlikely to be recorded for posterity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: accounts of battles, sacrifices to Muses by Lacedaemonians to ensure notable acts are recorded. Practical implication: do not expect a register or history to immortalize typical courageous acts.
